name: Descheduler
tagline: evicts pods that should be running somewhere else
author: K8s Dockside
description:
The descheduler evicts running pods so the scheduler can place them again somewhere better: off an over-used node, away from a duplicate of themselves, off a node whose taints they no longer tolerate. It has no custom resources and no API — it is a CronJob or a Deployment, a policy in a ConfigMap, and a trail of Events on the pods it evicted. That is exactly what this plugin reads.

The overview says whether it is installed and how it runs — schedule or interval, dry run or not, which version — and what it has actually done lately. Activity is the log: every eviction it recorded, live, with the plugin that asked for it, the node the pod left, and the failures alongside the successes, because an eviction refused by a PodDisruptionBudget is the interesting one. Policy is the settings, as forms rather than YAML: every plugin with a plain sentence on what it does, thresholds and limits as fields, and the file it would write shown before anything is applied — through the app's own confirmation.

Pods get a panel saying whether this pod could be evicted at all, worked out from the DefaultEvictor settings actually in the policy, and nodes get one for what left them recently.

charts.label: Pods evicted, by plugin
charts.description: Evictions in the hour up to each point, from descheduler's own descheduler_pods_evicted_total counter. Needs a Prometheus scraping the descheduler; 0.34 and older only export descheduler_pods_evicted.

charts.label: Evictions attempted, by result
charts.description: The same counter split by result, so refused evictions show up beside the successful ones.

charts.label: Descheduling cycle, 90th percentile
charts.description: How long a full pass over the cluster takes, from descheduler_loop_duration_seconds.

actions.label: Allow descheduling
actions.confirm: Annotate {namespace}/{name} with descheduler.alpha.kubernetes.io/evict? The descheduler may then evict it even where its own rules would normally protect it.

actions.done: {name} is back to the ordinary rules
